rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The recurring prophetic appeal is an earnest, affectionate final warning: the people still have time to abandon wrongdoing and follow their messenger rather than corrupt leaders.
rows.anchor: These words serve to remind and caution the nation in a very earnest and affectionate way in the last phase.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hūd points to visible favors rather than divine power or majesty: wealth, children, orchards and springs should lead to gratitude and obedience, not neglect of the Hereafter or tyranny.
rows.anchor: are meant to warn his nation with regard to God’s favours instead of His power and majesty.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The horrible day Hūd fears is the punishment that necessarily comes upon a people who deny their messenger.
rows.anchor: This refers to the punishment that necessarily visits a nation guilty of denying its messenger.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: True knowledge of God makes people fear His favors even more than His trials, lest they fail their duty and the blessings make them heedless; few understand this.
rows.anchor: People who have a true comprehension of God fear His favours more than His trials

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The reply about whether Hūd should counsel them is sarcastic: they dismiss his concern for their future as madness and refuse to value his sympathy.
rows.anchor: they too conceal a kind of sarcasm in them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A person may ignore a well-wisher’s advice yet still value the concern and want counsel; Hūd’s people instead rejected both the advice and the well-wisher’s goodwill.
rows.anchor: He in fact wants to be counselled whether he pays heed to it or not.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hūd’s people call the punishment warning an old bluff, claiming it was threatened before without coming and will not come now; the Qur’an gives parallel denials at 23:83 and 27:68.
rows.anchor: They commented that this threat of punishment is nothing new. It has also been sounded in the past

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Warnings of worldly and afterlife punishment have always been delivered, but negligent people treat the afterlife warning as a hoax because it is repeated without immediate fulfillment.
rows.anchor: there has never existed a period in this world when the warners have not warned negligent people of worldly as well as next-worldly punishment.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: People also fail to learn from worldly destructions, which their intellectuals explain away as ordinary turns of fortune unrelated to faith or belief.
rows.anchor: Intellectuals of their time regarded them to be the vicissitudes of time that happen to nations.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The recurring closing verses console the Prophet and warn his audience: the destruction of Hūd’s people is a clear sign, though deniers make excuses to evade faith.
rows.anchor: The repetitive verses carry assurance for the Prophet (sws) and warning for his addressees.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God grants deniers a respite under His established practice, but they cannot ultimately escape His grasp.
rows.anchor: People who adopt this attitude are given a certain respite according to God’s established practice but can never escape His grasp.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The prophets’ messages, their peoples’ responses and their fates are alike; since Quraysh show the same attitude toward their messenger, their fate cannot differ.
rows.anchor: The Quraysh too are now guilty of the same attitude with their messenger. So how can their fate be different!

words: إِذْ قَالَ لَهُمْ أَخُوهُمْ صَٰلِحٌ أَلَا تَتَّقُونَ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṣāliḥ’s opening appeal repeats the formulation used at the end of the preceding prophetic account, where it was already explained.
rows.anchor: Precisely these verses have been mentioned at end of the last anecdote and they have been explained there.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṣāliḥ declares that he is no false prophet or bluffer but God’s trustworthy messenger, faithfully conveying His message.
rows.anchor: Ṣāliḥ (sws) said that he is not a false prophet and is not bluffing them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command to fear God and obey Ṣāliḥ warns against following deviant leaders and reminds the people that the horrific day is near.
rows.anchor: The words “so, fear God and obey me” sound a warning to these people.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The prophets’ open refusal of personal gain serves public welfare: they come to give people truth, not take anything from them, and such selflessness has spread truth widely.
rows.anchor: Lack of personal gain is an important condition for public welfare.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṣāliḥ’s introductory warning says worldly success blinds his people to danger; their apparent prosperity is actually an alarm of sudden death, a lesson also developed through Hūd’s people.
rows.anchor: Ṣāliḥ (sws) warned them that this apparent prosperity is fooling them; it is in fact an alarm for sudden death.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Like Hūd’s people, those who fail to thank God for favors receive a respite they mistake for good, until a horrific storm ends it.
rows.anchor: if people do not show gratitude on the favours given to them, they are given respite

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṣāliḥ raised this warning while his people were at the height of their development.
rows.anchor: when his people were at the pinnacle of their development.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase about what is here refers to the people’s prosperous condition, which the following words spell out.
rows.anchor: refer to the state of prosperity of his people. Succeeding words explain it.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Favors are entrusted gifts, not personal rights; the greater a person’s privilege, the greater the need for gratitude and vigilance rather than complacent enjoyment.
rows.anchor: Favours are not rights of people. They are entrusted to them by the Giver.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an argues for the Hereafter from God’s providence: every privilege entails accountability, as human reason and nature attest, and only corrupted nature and intellect deny it.
rows.anchor: The Qur’ ān has argued at a number of instances in favour of the Hereafter on the basis of God’s providence.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Their clusters are tightly packed” describes bunches of grapes that are closely knit and intertwined.
rows.anchor: bunches of grapes that are closely-knit and intertwined.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Arabs’ ideal orchard combined grapes and pomegranates above flowing canals, crops in the middle and dense date palms at the borders; naming these favors prompts the question of accountability, a reality also repeated in the Gospels.
rows.anchor: to the Arabs the most cherished orchard was one which had grapes and pomegranates with canals flowing beneath it;

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The orchard’s owner will hold its recipients accountable for its favors rather than leave them unaccountable.
rows.anchor: the owner of this orchard will remain aloof and not hold them accountable for these favours

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word describing their mountain carving means happy, absorbed and arrogant; it marks a short-sighted state and has the same connotation at 15:82.
rows.anchor: to be happy, engrossed and arrogant.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Thamūd were skilled at carving mountain structures, and their wealthy people built edifices and castles to outdo one another, as the ‘Ād had done.
rows.anchor: It is evident from history that the Tham ūd had attained great heights in carving out buildings from rocky structures and mountains.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Conspicuous spending to assert superiority reflects indifference to God and the Hereafter; the resulting society neglects public welfare and is short-lived under God’s laws, soon becoming ruins.
rows.anchor: Spending wealth in an exorbitant way to express superiority is due to indifference to God and the Hereafter.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṣāliḥ warns that their impressive structures will not last because their respite is nearly over.
rows.anchor: He told them these structures they are building will not remain forever. Their respite is about to end.
